summary: Describes version 2 of the Host Access Protocol as implemented in the Terrestrial Wideband Network (TWBNET). It is informational and documents a specific network's protocol, not a standard.

eli5.summary: This describes how computers connect to one particular research network.

questions: what is the host access protocol
what is hap in the terrestrial wideband network
what is the difference between hap datagrams and streams
how does hap acceptance refusal flow control work
subtitle: The network-layer protocol hosts used to reach the Terrestrial Wideband Network, with datagrams, guaranteed streams and multicast groups.

tldr.problem: Hosts attached to the Wideband networks needed a defined way to exchange data and control messages with their local packet switch, including bandwidth-guaranteed traffic for things like voice.
tldr.mechanism: HAP defines datagram and stream data messages plus link control messages over the host-to-switch link. A Service Agent inside the switch allocates streams and multicast groups through Setup exchanges, and an acceptance/refusal mechanism gives optional flow control.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1221 documents version 2 of this developmental protocol as used in the TWBNET. It is informational, it obsoletes most but not all of RFC 907, and it is not an Internet standard.

facts.label: Status message interval
facts.value: Once a second; restart after 10 seconds of silence

today: RFC 1221 is an Informational memo, not an Internet standard. It updates RFC 907 and obsoletes most but not all of it, and it describes a developmental protocol used in the TWBNET.

sections.title: What HAP Is
sections.content:
The Host Access Protocol (HAP) is a network layer protocol (ISO layer 3 lower), below the Internet Protocol and above any link layer protocol. It defines the host-to-network control messages and host-to-host data messages exchanged over the access link between a host and its packet switch node, called a Wideband Packet Switch (WPS). It was first implemented for the Wideband Packet Satellite Network (WBNET), and RFC 1221 describes it as used in the Terrestrial Wideband Network (TWBNET).

HAP is full duplex and nonreliable, with an optional flow control mechanism. It offers two data services. Datagrams are variable length, unsequenced, independent messages with no guaranteed delivery. Streams are built on top of that and give bandwidth guarantees, but need explicit setup and teardown. Each type of message can be up to 2048 octets. Every host has a permanent 16-bit logical address, and multicast is supported through group addresses.

The memo says HAP is a developmental protocol that will be revised. This version was prompted by the move to non-broadcast T1 fiber links, the need to carry upper protocols other than IP, such as DECNET Phase V, ST and CLNP, and the wish to simplify interaction with ST2 (RFC 1190).
sections.eli5: HAP is how a computer hands messages to the network box it is plugged into. It has an ordinary lane, where messages may get lost, and a reserved lane for things that need steady speed.

sections.title: Datagram and Stream Headers
sections.content:
Every HAP message is made of 16-bit words. Word 0 identifies the message type and word 1 is a header checksum, the 2's-complement of the 2's-complement sum of the other header words. A message whose header checksum does not match must be discarded.

A datagram header (words 0 to 6) carries a Go-Priority advisory, an 8-bit message number, a discard flag, a data error flag, a 2-bit priority (low, medium, high), a time-to-live designator (1, 2, 5 or 10 seconds), a reliability level, a reliability length, destination and source host addresses, and a Protocol ID for the next higher protocol. The data is up to 2048 octets and must be an even number of octets.

A stream message has the same shape, except that the type, time to live and reliability are fixed when the stream is created, and a 10-bit stream ID replaces them. All stream messages have priority over any datagram message, and stream priority does not change the order of delivery.

The reliability field selects one of four forward error correction levels (low, medium-low, medium-high, high). The reliability length lets a host send private headers, such as IP and TCP headers, at the highest reliability while the rest of the data uses the chosen level.
sections.eli5: Each message starts with a label showing where it goes, how important it is and how carefully to protect it. A quick check number lets the network throw away any label that got scrambled.

sections.title: Acceptance and Refusal
sections.content:
The acceptance/refusal (A/R) mechanism is the optional flow control. The host turns it on for a link with a bit in the Restart Complete message. Each message carries an 8-bit message number that is incremented modulo 256, skipping zero, because zero means A/R is disabled for that message. Up to 127 messages may be outstanding in each direction.

A receiver that cannot accept a message returns a refusal with the message number and a reason code. Sample codes include 1 (source WPS congestion), 3 (destination host dead) and 11 (message length too long). Acceptances can ride on data going the other way or in a separate control message. An acceptance of message N implicitly accepts earlier outstanding messages, and several A/R words can be aggregated into one control message. An acceptance is not an end-to-end acknowledgement and guarantees nothing about delivery.

The A/R mechanism can be disabled for a pure discard interface. Critical feedback can then still travel in an Unnumbered Response control message. The Go-Priority field separately tells a sender which priorities are currently being accepted.
sections.eli5: It is like a clerk saying 'got it' or 'sorry, I cannot take that right now, and here is why'. Saying 'got it' to the tenth letter also covers the nine before it.

sections.title: The Service Agent: Streams and Groups
sections.content:
Resources such as streams and groups are allocated by exchanging Setup messages, carried as datagrams with Protocol ID 1, with the Service Agent at network address zero. A host-initiated setup is a three-way exchange: Setup Request, Setup Reply, Setup Acknowledgment. The host should expect a reply within 3 seconds and should acknowledge within one second. The Service Agent can also send Notifications, for example that a stream was suspended or a group was deleted, which the host acknowledges. Information Request and Reply messages let a host find out which resources it owns, which is useful after a crash or reboot.

A stream is created with a Create Stream Request that sets properties such as data words per interval, the interval, reliability, precedence (low, medium, high) and the destination list. A higher precedence stream can preempt a lower one at setup time. A host asking for less bandwidth should slow down immediately, but one asking for more must wait for the reply. Unused streams may be deleted after a 6 minute interval if the owner is down or unreachable.

A group is a multicast address. The network duplicates messages to all members except the sender. When a group is created, the Service Agent returns a 48-bit key with the 16-bit group address. Other hosts must present the key to join, which the memo says minimizes the chance of unwanted members. How the key is distributed is outside HAP.
sections.eli5: To reserve the fast lane, you fill in a form at the clerk's desk saying how much room you need, and the clerk confirms. To make a group mailing address, the clerk gives you a secret code that others must show to join.

sections.title: Link Monitoring and Restart
sections.content:
Once a second, the host and WPS exchange Status messages carrying traffic and error counts, and the WPS reports them to the Network Operations Center. If either side hears no Status message for ten seconds, the link is restarted.

Restart uses a Restart Request (RR) and Restart Complete (RC) exchange. Both ends must have sent and received an RC before the link is up. The state diagram has five states: OFF, INIT, RR-SNT, RC-SNT and ON, and every state has a 10-second timeout back to OFF. A restart zeroes the monitoring statistics and stops traffic in both directions.

Other control messages cover loopback requests for fault diagnosis, a Link Going Down message that a side should send before it voluntarily disables a link, and a No Operation message of up to 32 words of arbitrary data.
sections.eli5: The two sides keep saying 'still here?' every second. If one goes quiet for ten seconds, they both start over with a polite handshake before talking again.

sections.title: Compatibility and Future Extensions
sections.content:
Version 0 of HAP had no Protocol ID field. An IL bit instead said whether an IP header followed. The WPS tells versions apart from the version number in the Restart messages and converts messages for version 0 hosts, which probably lowers their maximum throughput. Version 1 uses Protocol IDs, where 0 means no higher level header, 256 to 511 are ISO protocols and 1500 to 65535 match Ether-type numbers.

The earlier 'Group Streams' feature was removed because no known applications used it. The memo lists two possible future additions that TWBNET does not support: a 'conference' resource and 'shared streams'. It says security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: The new version still knows how to talk to older computers by translating their old labels. A couple of fancier features are only ideas for later.

fields.name: LB
fields.desc: Loopback indicator: 0 sent by host, 1 sent by WPS.

fields.name: Message Number
fields.desc: Used by A/R; zero disables A/R for this message.

fields.name: Header Checksum
fields.desc: 2's-complement of the 2's-complement sum of words 0-6, excluding itself.

fields.name: Piggybacked A/R
fields.desc: Optional A/R word for opposite-direction traffic; zero means none.

fields.name: Destination Host Address
fields.desc: Logical address of the destination host.

fields.name: Source Host Address
fields.desc: Logical address of the source host.
